extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, congressional staff, patent practitioners, and patent stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and codifies procedural rules and substantive criteria in amendments to the Patent Reform Act of 2007, including congressional review of USPTO regulations, publication/opt-out provisions, and a mandated study of patent damages. Focused on legislative requirements and investigatory criteria for patent policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Date of USPTO Regulations — 60-day Congressional Review
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation promulgated by the United States Patent and Trademark Office under section 2(b)(2) of title 35, United States Code, with respect to any matter described in section 2(c)(6) of such title, may not take effect before the end of a period of 60 days beginning on the date on which the Under Secretary of Commerce for Intellectual Property and Director of the United States Patent and Trademark Office submits to each House of Congress a copy of the regulation, together with a report containing the reasons for its adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation and report so submitted shall be referred to the Committee on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives and the Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Resolution of Disapproval — Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: If a joint resolution of disapproval with respect to the regulation is enacted into law, the regulation shall not become effective or continue in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides Congress the ability to nullify a USPTO regulation via joint resolution enacted into law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Resolution Defined (Required Wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of this subsection, the term a 'joint resolution of disapproval' means a joint resolution, the matter after the resolving clause of which is as follows: 'That Congress disapproves the regulation submitted by the Under Secretary of Commerce for Intellectual Property and Director of the United States Patent and Trademark Office on ___ relating to ___, and such regulation shall have no force or effect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first blank is for the date and the second blank for a description of the regulation at issue — specifying exact statutorily required language for a valid disapproval resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral of Joint Resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint resolution of disapproval shall be referred in the House of Representatives to the Committee on the Judiciary and in the Senate to the Committee on the Judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets committee referral paths for congressional consideration of disapproval resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floor Consideration Timing for Joint Resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A vote on final passage of a joint resolution of disapproval shall be taken in each House on or before the close of the 15th day after the bill or resolution is reported by the committee of that House to which it was referred or after such committee has been discharged from further consideration of the joint resolution of disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposes a fixed deadline (15 days after committee report or discharge) for floor action on disapproval resolutions to ensure timely consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Inferences from Congressional Inaction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Congress does not enact a joint resolution of disapproval, no court or agency may infer therefrom any intent of the Congress with regard to such regulation or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents judicial or administrative inference of congressional approval from mere inaction on a disapproval resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of Days for Review and Consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The 60-day period referred to in paragraph (1) and the 15-day period referred to in paragraph (5) shall be computed by excluding— the days on which either House of Congress is not in session because of an adjournment of the Congress sine die; and any Saturday and Sunday, not excluded under subparagraph (A), when either House is not in session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies how to count calendar days for statutory review deadlines by excluding certain adjournments and weekends when either House is not in session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Rulemaking Authority Clause
rubrics_metrics.description: This subsection is enacted by the Congress as an exercise of the rulemaking power of the Senate and House of Representatives respectively, and as such it is deemed a part of the rules of each House, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressly frames the review mechanism as an exercise of each House's internal rulemaking power, incorporating the procedure into House and Senate rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of Opt-Out / Secrecy via Second Office Action and 90-Day Discard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under this provision, if you receive your second and usually final rejection and you say, okay, within 90 days I’m going to discard my patent, that wrapper is not available to anyone. It remains a secret and you’re allowed to keep your trade secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that choosing the 'second office action' option preserves an applicant's ability to keep the application secret (opt-out) until disposition: the second (usually final) rejection and then a 90-day window to discard to maintain secrecy; also notes Issa's rationale that the second office action choice gives an effectively unlimited period to pursue up to two rejections (subject to 20-year patent term).

rubrics_metrics.name: 1999 Publication Requirement and Opt-Out Under Existing Law
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1999 Patent Act required the Patent Office to publish on the Internet a patent application 18 months from the date of filing; under current law, you can opt out of that (so you can protect your invention and not have it published).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text and debate note that elimination of the opt-out provision in the bill would be a major change from existing law and carries risks to applicants (exposure to foreign competitors), making preservation or modification of opt-out a substantive policy criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study on Patent Damages — General Requirement and Timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: The Under Secretary of Commerce for Intellectual Property and Director of the United States Patent and Trademark Office shall conduct a study of patent damage awards in cases where such awards have been based on a reasonable royalty under section 284 of title 35, United States Code. The study should, at a minimum, consider cases from 1990 to the present. Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Director shall submit to the Congress a report on the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandates an empirical, time-bounded study and report to Congress to inform potential legislative or other reforms related to damages and reasonable royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Criterion 1 — Trend Analysis of Reasonable-Royalty Awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the mean or median dollar amount of reasonable-royalty-based patent damages awarded by courts or juries, as the case may be, has significantly increased on a per case basis during the period covered by the study, taking into consideration adjustments for inflation and other relevant economic factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directs the study to perform econometric or statistical trend analysis, controlling for inflation and other economic influences, to assess whether damages per case have risen materially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Criterion 2 — Pattern of Excessive or Inequitable Awards and Contributing Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there has been a pattern of excessive and inequitable reasonable-royalty-based damages during the period covered by the study and, if so, any contributing factors, including, for example, evidence that Federal courts have routinely and inappropriately broadened the scope of the 'entire market value rule', or that juries have routinely misapplied the entire market value rule to the facts at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires analysis of doctrinal application (e.g., entire market value rule), jury behavior, and court decisions to identify systemic causes of potentially inappropriate awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Criterion 3 — Measures to Guard Against Inappropriate Awards
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent that a pattern of excessive and inequitable damage awards exists, measures that could guard against such inappropriate awards without unduly prejudicing the rights and remedies of patent holders or significantly increasing litigation costs, including legislative reforms or improved model jury instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directs the study to propose remedies (legislative or procedural) and evaluate their tradeoffs between reducing inappropriate awards and preserving patent holder rights and manageable litigation costs; suggests model jury instructions as a candidate measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Criterion 4 — Evaluate Apportionment-Related Legislative Proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent that a pattern of excessive and inequitable damage awards exists, whether legislative proposals that would mandate, or create a presumption in favor of, apportionment of reasonable-royalty-based patent damages would effectively guard against such inappropriate awards without unduly prejudicing the rights and remedies of patent holders or significantly increasing litigation costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically tasks the study with assessing apportionment mandates or presumptions as potential fixes and their effects on rights and costs.
